Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

Vignette:
Adebola, at eighty years old, still moved with the quiet authority she had cultivated over a five-decade career as a policy analyst. Widowed for a decade, her work was her anchor, a world of logic and reason that she commanded with precision. That world fractured six months ago, on a frigid Tuesday in February. The memory of the collision does not exist for her as a coherent narrative, but as a series of intensely vivid, disconnected sensory snapshots. There is no recollection of the sound of the impact, only a profound silence where it should be. Instead, she remembers the sudden, overwhelming smell of whiskey wafting from the other car just before the world spun—a smell she now understands came from the drunk driver who ran the red light. She has a crystal-clear image of the passenger-side window blooming into a spiderweb of cracks, and then the distinct, biting cold of the crumpled metal door pressing hard against her arm. That sensation is followed by the acrid, choking smell of burning engine oil, a smell that filled her lungs as she drifted in and out of consciousness. The moments connecting these fragments are a complete blank, a void her mind refuses to enter.

In the weeks that followed, Adebola believed she was simply recovering from the physical injuries. But the sensory fragments of the crash began to intrude on her life, ambushing her without warning. One morning, a piece of toast caught in her toaster, and the wisps of smoke that curled into her kitchen sent her staggering back against the counter, heart hammering against her ribs, the phantom smell of burning oil thick in her throat. At her office, a junior colleague used an alcohol-based hand sanitizer, and the sharp scent instantly conjured the other driver’s face, a fleeting image she immediately shoves away, a mental reflex that leaves her breathless and disoriented. She finds herself doing this constantly—pushing the memory away the second a fragment appears, terrified of what might happen if she lets the sequence play out to completion.

Her carefully ordered life has become a minefield of potential threats. She had come to believe that her own strong emotions were dangerous; a surge of anger at a political commentator or a wave of grief for her late husband now felt like a precursor to a total loss of control, a sign that the horror was about to swallow her whole. The world outside her apartment became similarly menacing. She began working almost exclusively from home, unable to tolerate the sudden movements of her colleagues in the open-plan office. A person reaching quickly for a book or turning abruptly in the hallway would cause her to flinch, her body bracing for an impact. What frightened her most were the moments when the past simply replaced the present. Last week, while reading in her armchair, she suddenly felt the distinct, biting cold on her right arm again, as if the mangled car door were pressing into her flesh. She looked down and saw only the sleeve of her cardigan, but the sensation was so real, so absolute, that she cried out, feeling utterly trapped within the walls of her own home.

The isolation and relentless vigilance have taken a toll. She missed her granddaughter’s piano recital last month because the thought of getting into a car, even as a passenger, was unbearable. The pained understanding in her daughter’s voice over the phone felt like a new kind of injury. It was this growing distance from her family, coupled with the terror of the flashbacks, that finally propelled her to seek help. Adebola, a woman who had built a life on intellect and control, now feels besieged by her own mind. She is terrified that these fragments will one day consume her entirely, trapping her forever in the wreckage of that February evening. Her hope is not grand; it is simply to feel a sense of safety in her own skin again, to be able to smell toast or feel a cool breeze without being thrown back into the worst moment of her life.
